item.title: Can You Wake Up Speaking a Different Accent?
item.description:
Cognition

Can You Wake Up Speaking a Different Accent?

The surprising science of Foreign Accent Syndrome.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Foreign Accent Syndrome can make people sound foreign without learning a new language or accent.
  • Brain changes can alter speech patterns, creating the illusion of a different accent.
  • Listeners often perceive familiar speech changes as foreign accents, revealing how we process voices.

When Kay Russell woke from a short nap one evening, she no longer sounded like herself. The 49-year-old from Gloucestershire had gone to sleep with her usual English accent. She awoke sounding unmistakably French. She had never lived in France, wasn’t pretending, and hadn’t forgotten how to speak English. Overnight, her accent had seemingly changed.

As extraordinary as it sounds, Kay isn’t alone. Around the world, people have reported waking from sleep, emerging from surgery, or recovering from illness only to discover that they suddenly sound as though they come from another country. An Oregon woman awoke from routine dental surgery with what listeners described as an Irish accent. A Virginia woman who had never learned Russian began speaking English with a Russian accent. After a stroke, one English woman’s Geordie accent was perceived as Jamaican.

Can you really wake up speaking with a different accent? In rare cases, yes, but not for the reasons you might think.

The condition is known as Foreign Accent Syndrome (FAS), an exceptionally rare neurological speech disorder in which changes to a person’s speech make them sound as though they have suddenly acquired a foreign accent. (McWhirter, et al., 2019) The effect is so convincing that listeners often assume the speaker has come from somewhere else, even though they are speaking their native language.

An Accent Without a Country

One of the most famous early cases involved a Norwegian woman, known as “Astrid,” who suffered a head injury during a bombing raid during World War II. After recovering, she spoke Norwegian with what listeners perceived as a strong German accent. Tragically, during the German occupation, this left her socially ostracized by her own community. (Stollznow, 2026)

One of the more unusual reported cases involved the late singer George Michael. After surviving a severe bout of pneumonia and spending weeks in a coma, he awoke to find his familiar North London accent had apparently been replaced by a pronounced West Country twang. (Jonkers, et al., 2017) The change was temporary, disappearing after only a few days, but it offered a fascinating example of how neurological disruption can alter the way a person’s voice is perceived.

Other documented cases include Americans who suddenly sound British, British speakers who appear to have French accents, Spanish speakers who are mistaken for Hungarians, and Japanese speakers perceived as sounding Korean. These aren’t people who have somehow downloaded a new accent overnight. Something much more interesting is happening.

The Brain Hasn’t Learned a New Accent

Despite its name, Foreign Accent Syndrome isn’t really about acquiring a foreign accent at all. Most cases follow neurological injury, including stroke, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, seizures, or dementia. The damage subtly alters the mechanics of speech production. Typically, it involves subtle changes in pronunciation, rhythm, intonation, and speech stress, a pattern known as dysprosody.

article continues after advertisement

Listeners naturally try to make sense of these changes by matching them to accents they already know. In other words, the “foreign accent” exists largely in the ear of the listener. If someone loses the ability to pronounce certain sounds while overemphasizing others, our brains instinctively categorize the resulting speech: That sounds French. That sounds Russian. That sounds Australian. But no genuine French, Russian, or Australian accent has been acquired. Instead, the brain has lost some of the fine motor control that previously produced the speaker’s familiar accent.

It’s a bit like hearing a few notes of a melody and instantly believing you recognize the tune, even when you’re mistaken. Our brains are remarkably good at finding familiar patterns, even when they’re not there.

Living With a Different Voice

Although Foreign Accent Syndrome often attracts sensational headlines, the reality is far less amusing for those who experience it. An accent is part of our identity. It reflects where we grew up, the communities we belong to, and the people around us. When that familiar voice suddenly changes, people may feel as though they’ve lost part of themselves.

Patients frequently report frustration when strangers question where they’re “really” from. Family members sometimes say they sound like an entirely different person. The disconnect between how speakers hear themselves and how others perceive them can be deeply distressing.

Importantly, the condition doesn’t affect intelligence or thought. People know exactly what they want to say and are fully aware that their speech has changed. They simply can’t produce it in quite the same way.

Some people recover within days or weeks, while others continue to speak with altered speech patterns for years, depending on the extent and location of the neurological damage. Treatment typically focuses on the underlying neurological condition, alongside speech-language therapy to improve speech production and communication. (Utianski and Bridge, 2024) Although outcomes vary widely, many people experience partial or complete recovery.

article continues after advertisement

What Accents Reveal About the Mind

Foreign Accent Syndrome reminds us that accents are not simply permanent features of who we are. They emerge from the extraordinarily complex coordination of breathing, muscle movement, timing, and auditory feedback that allows us to produce fluent speech. Tiny disruptions to this system can produce surprisingly large changes in how others perceive us.

Perhaps that’s why the syndrome continues to fascinate neurologists and linguists alike. It reminds us that speech is one of the brain’s most sophisticated achievements, even though we produce it effortlessly every day. Most of us never stop to think about how our accent is created, or how closely it is tied to our sense of self. Foreign Accent Syndrome offers a rare window into both.

item.title: When Death Awareness Changes How We See the Body
item.description:
Body Image

When Death Awareness Changes How We See the Body

How mortality shapes body image, objectification, and self-worth.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Awareness of mortality can heighten discomfort with the body’s animal, vulnerable nature.
  • Cultural beauty standards may help people distance themselves from aging, illness, and death.
  • Healthier death awareness can foster respect for the body without tying worth to appearance.
Source: Alexander Krivitskiy / Unsplash

The human body presents us with a psychological contradiction. It’s the source of movement, identity, pleasure, intimacy, and life itself... and yet it also ages, sweats, bleeds, becomes ill, and eventually dies. The same body that makes existence possible consistently reminds us that existence is temporary.

Psychologists studying terror management theory have examined what happens when this contradiction becomes tough to ignore. The theory proposes that, as humans, we manage the anxiety created by knowing we will die through cultural beliefs, identities, achievements, and standards that make life feel meaningful and enduring. A large meta-analysis found that reminders of mortality can influence our judgments and behavior, mostly on an unconscious level. We aren’t typically aware of the ways death can drive our thoughts and actions.

One especially provocative branch of this research concerns creatureliness: our awareness that, despite our smarts, culture, and carefully curated LinkedIn profiles, we are really just animals with vulnerable biological bodies.

The Body as an Existential Reminder

In a series of influential experiments, psychologist Jamie Goldenberg and colleagues proposed that people psychologically distance themselves from animals partly because animals remind us of physical vulnerability and death. When mortality was made salient (brought to awareness), participants showed a stronger preference for descriptions depicting humans as distinct from other animals.

This doesn’t mean that every uncomfortable reaction to the body hides a conscious fear of death; the proposed process is subtler. When the body’s animal qualities become obvious—like sweating, aging, or getting sick with the flu—they may weaken the reassuring idea that human beings are elevated above nature and destined for some form of symbolic permanence.

The result is an interesting ambivalence. We may value the body when it supports the “preferred” culturally admired qualities like beauty, fitness, discipline, youth, or sexual desirability—while becoming uncomfortable with bodily functions that expose the “distasteful” things like dependency, disorder, aging, and mortality.

Research has found that mortality reminders can increase investment in the body when physical appearance already serves as a source of self-esteem. In one set of studies, participants with relatively high body esteem responded to mortality salience with greater identification with their bodies or increased interest in sex. Said differently, the body can become reassuring when it confirms that we meet whatever cultural standards we personally value.

But when the body fails to provide that reassurance—or when its stark physicality becomes a little too prominent—the reaction can reverse.

Why Women’s Bodies Carry an Extra Burden

Source: Jeferson Santu / Unsplash

These dynamics have particular consequences for women because women’s bodies have historically been subjected to more intensive appearance monitoring, sexual evaluation, and cultural expectations.

Goldenberg notes that women’s menstruating, lactating, pregnant, and childbearing bodies make human creatureliness unusually visible. At the same time, cultural representations frequently transform women into polished visual objects: beautiful, controlled, wrinkle-free, youthful, and somehow untouched by the messiness of biology. Objectification may therefore accomplish something psychologically paradoxical. It emphasizes the female body while simultaneously stripping it of many qualities that make it recognizably living, vulnerable, and human.

A frequently cited experiment illustrates this process. Participants encountered a woman who either appeared to have dropped a tampon from her handbag or a hair clip. The reminder of menstruation produced more negative reactions toward her; among participants who strongly endorsed conventional gender schemas, it also increased the tendency to objectify women more generally.

The researchers described this as a form of “feminine protection”: psychologically restoring an idealized, sanitized image of femininity after being reminded of the female body’s biological reality.

This framework may also help explain why culturally acceptable femininity is often associated with the awkward concealment of bodily processes. Women are expected to menstruate without evidence, age without appearing older, give birth and “bounce back,” experience menopause without inconvenience, and remain desirable without seeming too physically or sexually autonomous.

The idealized female body is permitted to be visible, and the fully creaturely female body is often expected to remain discreet.

Mortality, Thinness, and Appearance Control

Death awareness may also intensify efforts to make the body conform to cultural ideals. In one study, reminders of mortality affected women’s intentions to restrict their eating differently depending on their body mass index. The findings suggested that, for some participants, controlling food intake offered a way to check the box on culturally rewarded standards of thinness when mortality was brought to mind.

Other experiments found that women who already placed significant value on their appearances could respond more positively to objectifying imagery or appearance-focused feedback after being reminded of death. If physical attractiveness has become an important source of worth, objectification may sometimes feel validating—even while reinforcing the system that reduces a person to her appearance.

This is one reason body ideals can be so psychologically powerful. They aren’t simply about aesthetic preferences; they may become entangled with identity, belonging, value, and the wish to feel protected from vulnerability.

Making Peace With Creatureliness

Source: Olenka Kotyk / Unsplash

The research doesn’t suggest that death awareness inevitably leads to body shame or sexism. It suggests that mortality can magnify whichever cultural standards we use to establish worth.

A healthier response may involve refusing the false choice between the body as an attractive object and the body as an embarrassing animal vessel. We aren't elevated minds burdened by inconvenient bodies. It's through our physicality that we love, work, laugh, create, move, comfort, and participate in our lives.

A body doesn’t need to remain young, perfectly maintained, or culturally approved to have value. Its vulnerability is evidence of life, not failure.

Maybe a more mature death awareness asks us not to rise above creatureliness, but to inhabit it more honestly: to respect the body without worshipping its appearance, and to care for it without imagining that the right amount of discipline will somehow make it immortal.

item.title: Why Aggression Can Be Good for Therapy
item.description:
Anger

Why Aggression Can Be Good for Therapy

The case for embracing and cultivating healthy aggression during therapy sessions.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Aggression is as important to the quality of one’s therapeutic work and career as love and empathy.
  • To know and integrate one’s own aggressive drives is to create the conditions for patients to do the same.
  • In the case of burnout, when good intentions do not inspire or sustain, aggression offers a powerful engine.

"Events of mutual aggression are unavoidable in the course of a life lived together, but, by the same token, the possibility of their clarification and resolution carries with it the possibility of further strengthening and deepening the relationship." (Kernberg, 2012, p. 288)

Aggression Isn't the Enemy in Therapy

There is a difference between “kind” and “nice.”

Therapists often resist their own aggression or insist on “niceness.” Yet doing so can actually impede patients’ awareness and expression of their own angry, dissatisfied feelings toward the therapist, which can thwart the integration of aggression into its healthy forms of realistic anger and assertiveness.

Instead, suppression of the therapist's aggression can drive a turn against the self, which some patients are apt to do in the form of shame and self-loathing as well as self-destructive behaviors. Thus, the illusion of a safe and constructive therapeutic relationship is preserved even as the harmful patterns for the patient are reinforced.

Stigmatizing therapist aggression insidiously fuels patients’ shame and defensiveness around their own feelings and impulses, making them harder to access and metabolize as part of themselves and their inner world. When any of us cannot access fundamental and emotion-laden parts of ourselves, we suffer in one way or another.

Moreover, the therapist’s aggression can be an important component to the aspects of therapy which require confronting patients’ maladaptive patterns and defenses and maintaining the therapeutic frame. Security with one’s own aggression actually lessens the risk of reactive, punishing confrontations (perhaps masked as “tough love”).

The regular recognition of and responsiveness to frustrated or hostile feelings encourages the therapist’s metabolism of these feelings, using them to understand themselves, the patient, and the process of the work, rather than unthinkingly acting them out. Still, it's important not to get ahead of ourselves—there are certainly instances where such acting out still happens for the most experienced therapists as enactments are generally considered a “when” rather than “if” clinical phenomenon.

It is not uncommon that therapists share the same fears as their patients when it comes to aggression—namely, that it is the destroyer of relationships—and so it is avoided in therapeutic relationships in similar measure as in personal ones. In reality, aggression in and of itself is not the enemy of connection, rather, it ensures that connection is imbued with vitality and the reality of our complex drives and feelings. In fact, Kernberg (1991) even emphasized the significance of aggression in romantic life as an integral element to gratifying sexual intimacy.

Aggression in Professional Life and Larger Context

Psychological health and stability rely on the integration of creative and destructive drives—libidinal and aggressive energy. Just as aggression is not the enemy of connection, nor is it the enemy of creation.

Our creative pursuits and value-driven goals need not be threatened by our aggression. Instead, efforts to suppress aggressive drives threaten to subdue passion, facilitate fatigue, and interfere with collegial relationships (which are much-needed sources of support and sustenance in their own right).

Healthy aggression can be seen in assertiveness as well as competition within one’s self or amongst peers, pushing us to grow. This is in contrast to aggression that is rejected, denied, and generally unintegrated, which is thought to drive envious and devaluing attitudes towards others. This type of aggression may be partly behind the seemingly rampant online practice of devaluing peers, positioning one’s self as superior in comparison:

  • “This new or specialized therapy solves all the problems that these other therapies have.”
  • “I’m better than all these other therapists because I do this instead of that and everyone who does 'that' is harmful or ineffective.”

Note the lack of nuance, context, or individualizing in statements of these kinds, which implicitly pit therapies and therapists against each other despite supposedly supporting the same aims of helping people in pain.

Disavowed aggression can also be an underlying issue for the therapist who appears “bland and uninvolved… [because they are] terrified of their own rageful feelings.” (Lunbeck, 2014, p. 73). Perhaps a provocative explanation in contrast to the more palatable “compassion fatigue,” which may also be accurate but potentially incomplete to understanding personal factors which contribute to fatigue.

We shouldn't, of course, overlook the systemic forces, including sociopolitical, economic, and institutional factors, that are absolutely implicated in the problem of therapist burnout. Therapists’ collective permission and encouragement to connect with and foster natural aggressive sources of energy do not pardon those forces, but rather offer sustenance in the face of them, maybe even energy to organize together and engage in advocacy efforts.

In short, we can and should look to aggression for resilience to burnout. Our values guide what we want to invest in, but we must draw from varied sources of energy to support that investment.

Conclusion

To survive, to thrive, and to go on caring, therapists, like all people, need healthy aggression. In this case, healthy aggression refers to angry, passionate, competitive, conquering drives, feelings, fantasies, etc. which are integrated into one's inner world and self-concept. Due to the development of healthy aggression as being a process in one's inner life, the specific outward manifestations are likely (and welcomed) to be personal and culture-laden, rather than universal and prescribed.

Within the therapist role, it is easier to specifically identify how healthy aggression plays a role in effective treatment such as setting and maintaining the therapeutic frame, healthy interpersonal boundaries, respect for, rather than denial of, power dynamics, non-shaming or judgmental confrontations, and the kind of endurance and sturdiness which requires both a clinical and personal backbone.

In the broader overlapping personal and professional spaces, healthy aggression is better identified by attitudes and interpersonal functioning rather than specific behaviors-- as in, engagement in and relative comfort with competition and disagreement for the sake of growth and good practice, resistance to devaluing, admiration rather than envy, passion and liveliness versus deadness and disengagement, and so on.

When all is said and done, embracing aggression helps us to know and embrace ourselves and others more fully and remember that "fighting the good fight" indeed requires "fighting."

item.title: Death Puts Life in Perspective
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Death Puts Life in Perspective

A Personal Perspective: A death close to home is a stark reminder to lean into life.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • Death close to home brings perspective to living.
  • Losing someone to a sudden death is shocking and can lead to questioning one's own life.
  • Living vitally and joyfully is a deliberate daily choice.

Death has a very powerful way of putting living in perspective.

My neighbor died last Thursday evening. Only 30 minutes earlier, he had been blowing leaves in his garden. While he was blowing leaves, masking the bird song, I had to chuckle; it was 8:30 p.m. Blowing leaves always seemed to be his way of settling himself in the evening; I assumed it was part of his bedtime routine. I suppose it’s fitting that he was out there with his blower right before he took the ultimate rest.

Death is decidedly weird. One minute you’re up and living, even living well, as in David’s case, and the next minute you’re gone. For those of us left alive, it’s bizarre. How could life be so fleeting? How is it that the exit can be so fast and final?

For David, as for my grandfather many years ago (who also died while doing yard work), it was a quick passing—maybe even one to be envied. I know many people, including my mother, who suffered for years in humiliating decline before death finally ushered them into a more peaceful place. Those of us who go quickly are perhaps the blessed, the lucky ones. Better to get it over with in an instant than suffer years of decline.

Make a daily practice of living fully.
Source: Darby Bonomi

People say, life is short: Do the thing you want to do. Right now, that line feels painfully obvious. Usually that phrase is bandied about, offered up as a way to give ourselves permission to do the thing we want, like buy the horse or take the vacation or retire. I have experienced enough death in my life that now I am determined to heed the phrase. Do the thing now. Refrain from getting caught up in silly things, don't worry about the small stuff, and focus on being grateful for every single day regardless of what it brings.

The birds were singing this morning, just like they always do. The deer were out too, doing what deer do. Everyone was going on living, even though David isn’t. The day after David died, I didn’t feel much like doing anything. I mean, why bother doing anything when I’m just going to die too? My husband also will die, maybe before me. Who knows: It might be today or tomorrow. Whenever it is, it will be too soon. So, I was feeling: What’s the point? Living felt cruel in a way—just a waiting game until the universe decides your number is up.

Days have passed, and I’ve brightened up. I've thought a lot about David, and how he lived. He was a funny, pragmatic, and extremely kind guy. He was a terrific neighbor, the kind who brings you the best homemade apricot jam you will ever have, throws a line over the fence so that you can borrow some juice from his generator when the power goes out (again), and goes out walking his dogs, patrolling the neighborhood many times a day. David is the kind of guy who would have us all go on living, breathing, eating good jam, and patrolling.

Dave, I went out and did your walk today. I said hello to the hawks, the cottontails in the bushes, the deer, and the squirrels. They’re all good. We’re all good. We miss you a lot, and I am still enjoying your best jam yet. I hope heaven has as good a jam as yours. Thanks for all the love and the inspiration to keep doing the things.

item.title: AI Has Memory and Humans Have Consequences
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Has Memory and Humans Have Consequences

AI can be wrong and stay exactly the same—a person can't.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • The real gap between AI and human cognition is what happens after a judgment is made.
  • A consequence structure lets judgment reshape identity, something humans have and machines don't.
  • We can't test whether anything is truly at stake for AI's accuracy.
Source: Image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay.

Human intelligence and artificial intelligence don't differ simply in how they think. They differ in what happens after a thought is made. For years, I've called these two forms of cognition different axes, not different points on the same scale.

What Is the Difference?

Large language models function in tens of thousands of dimensions, finding meaning from geometry. A person works through time, finding meaning in memory and risk. The comparison people commonly seek, better or worse, smarter or dumber, misses the shape of the problem. Different is a claim that begs the question. Different how? And why should it matter enough to build an argument on?

What Doesn't Follow You Home

Ask a physician to read a scan. If she misses something, the error doesn't end when she leaves the room. It becomes part of what she carries into the next diagnosis. It's that nudge toward more caution or a call to a colleague she wouldn't have made the week before.

An example here is distinguished between witnessing a tragedy and causing one. Bernard Williams called the difference agent-regret. This is when the person who acted feels the outcome differently than anyone who merely watched it happen, even if neither could have known better at the time.

A model carries nothing forward. Ask it the same question twice and get two different answers, and no friction registers anywhere in the system. Nothing "inside the AI" was risked in producing it.

The Structure of Consequence

I want to give this difference a name. Call it a consequence structure: the architecture through which a judgment alters the future identity of the one who made it. Human cognition develops inside a consequence structure built from memory, responsibility, and the possibility of loss. Machine computation, however fluent, does not.

To be clear, this isn't a claim that AI is deceptive. It's a claim that AI stands outside a category human judgment has never managed to escape and this is a category of decisions that cost something to make.

The Record vs. the Scar

Long-term memory isn't the simple distinction people often assume it is. A record remembers, but a scar changes you. Give an LLM persistent memory across sessions and you've given it a record. And there's the key point: you haven't given it a stake.

A judgment doesn't just inform the next decision. It becomes part of who makes it. And in this context, AI has outputs and humans have biographies. The future version of me is partly determined by whether today's judgment succeeds or fails. In contrast, a trading algorithm shut down after repeated losses doesn't dread the shutdown. It just stops running. Whatever accountability that may exist was imposed on it from outside.

The Test We Haven't Built

We've built instruments to measure accuracy and instruments to benchmark reasoning. We know how to check the record. We don't yet know how to test for the scar.

Maybe that's the difference that matters most.

item.title: Old Wine in New Pixels? Skeptcism About the Simulation Hypothesis
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Old Wine in New Pixels? Skeptcism About the Simulation Hypothesis

What simulation belief may reveal about ourselves, more than reality.

Posted July 21, 2026

Key points
  • A 2026 poll found 22% of U.S. adults called a simulation at least somewhat likely.
  • Derealization is felt unreality with intact reality testing—not evidence of a simulation.
  • Psychosocial factors correlated with belief in the simulation hypothesis are largely unresearched.

If reality is a simulation, isn't the idea that reality is a simulation itself a simulation? Then reality must be real — correct? If only it were that simple.

Every age builds its cosmology from its most advanced machines while keeping the old myths running in the background. The clockmakers gave us a clockwork universe; the industrial age, a body and psyche engine of classical forces; now, in the age of computation, quantum mechanics, and AI, a growing number of thoughtful people suspect reality itself is a very sophisticated program.

It can scarcely be denied that the supreme goal of all theory is to make the irreducible basic elements as simple and as few as possible without having to surrender the adequate representation of a single datum of experience. — Albert Einstein (1933)

Nick Bostrom's argument is a trilemma: humanity likely goes extinct before a posthuman stage, posthuman civilizations rarely run ancestor simulations, or we are almost certainly in one (Bostrom, 2003) — which seems to presume what it sets out to prove. The cultural case is louder: Elon Musk puts the odds we live in "base reality" at "one in billions" (On with Kara Swisher, 2016); Neil deGrasse Tyson says the likelihood "may be very high" (American Museum of Natural History, 2016); The Matrix (Wachowski & Wachowski, 1999) made it a modern myth of repression and freedom — waking from a deception into a harsher but truer reality. The hypothesis moves the opposite way.

Take it seriously less for what it says about the cosmos than about us — perhaps a way to relieve the hardest problems, existence, meaning, mortality, by supposing none of it is real.

Suppose it is correct. For daily life it changes little — try telling the gas-station attendant you needn't pay because nothing is real — except in one respect: living things would not be alive as we take them to be. David Chalmers resists that conclusion. "Virtual reality is genuine reality," he writes, and "Life in virtual worlds can be as good, in principle, as life outside virtual worlds" (Chalmers, 2022, p. xviii). His point is not that a depiction and a person are identical, but that a well-realized virtual life could be genuine, not counterfeit. Even so, the view demands a concession: that the aliveness one knows from inside is, at bottom, computation, and the felt line between a living being and a remarkable rendering may have to go.

Suppose instead it is false. Then it is metaphysics carried as conviction, dressed in artificial intelligence and paired with the belief that machines too are alive — securing the irreality of the real, relieving us of the plain fact of being an animal in the world. A harsher explanation, but likelier; simpler, per Occam's razor.

Escape From Reality

The impulse to doubt the world — perhaps to escape physicality — is ancient, and wears many masks. Plato's cave is about education and knowledge, prisoners taking shadows for the real (Plato, ca. 375 BCE/1992, Book VII). Descartes' demon is a device of methodological skepticism (Descartes, 1641/1996, Meditation I). Putnam's brain in a vat concerns reference and skepticism, not cosmology (Putnam, 1981, ch. 1). Zhuangzi, unsure whether he dreamt he was a butterfly or was a butterfly dreaming him, explores perspective and transformation (Zhuangzi, 2013, ch. 2). Scholars read the simulation hypothesis along these lines — as a "new technoscientific religious narrative" (Virk, 2025).

To cast them all as teaching that reality is a dream does a disservice; but each asks whether appearances can deceive, in the deepest sense. The simulation hypothesis is the latest, most literal-minded entry — set apart by its scientistic wrapper, congruent with our technological metaphors. Yet older visions that relativized self or world usually bound the vision to an ethic, a discipline of compassion or care for how to live. This one carries no such code: it offers a metaphysics of unreality and leaves quite open how we treat one another. That gap is where it can grow dangerous.

Oddly little is known about who believes it, or why. The evidence is scant: a literature review found no validated scale or representative study of simulation belief; one 2026 commercial poll reported 22% of U.S. adults considered it at least somewhat likely (7% very, 15% somewhat), while 23% did not know the concept, openness skewing younger and male (Polls & Insights, 2026).

Separate two things: entertaining the hypothesis as an idea — a probability assigned over coffee — and the lived sense that the world is not quite real. Some experience the latter as derealization: a felt unreality in which reality testing remains intact (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). That is a symptom, not a position, and nothing here shows simulation belief is caused by derealization; at most the resemblance is a research question. My own suspicion, as interpretation not finding, is that the hypothesis can work as a projection — an inner unreality read outward onto the cosmos.

Death Be Not Proud

Beneath that may lie the denial of death. Ernest Becker argued that much of culture is machinery for holding mortality at bay (Becker, 1973); the hypothesis offers a modern version — not an afterlife but an ill-defined upperlife (if you will), a higher plane on which one is perhaps never quite alive, and so can never quite die.

Erich Fromm treated the tension between pro- and anti-life stances at length — largely around the last century's horrors and the uses of technology — through lenses we can apply here. He set biophilia, a love of the living, against a necrophilous orientation toward death, the nonliving, and the mechanical (Fromm, 1964, 1973). When does a computational metaphor become a preference for the mechanical over the living?

Recent research bears on this. One study tied existential nihilism to lower well-being in campus and online nihilism-community samples (Crammond et al., 2026); another found it predicted suicidal ideation among 775 students across three waves, even after accounting for meaning in life and depressive symptoms (Kyron et al., 2025). Neither shows simulation belief causes either outcome, but the overlap merits study.

If the world is only rendered, do other people become non-player characters toward whom cruelty costs nothing? One might prefer exit to repair; and where nothing is finally real, there is less common ground for truth and less demand for common humanity.

Stranger Danger

What can be said without more research is limited by epistemic humility. We are often manifestations of the very processes about which we are most curious. We can comprehend only what the human brain, augmented or otherwise, permits. To wonder whether reality is a simulation is itself a living, conscious act — yet to believe the hypothesis is perhaps in ways a matter of faith that sounds scientific.

The hypothesis has caught a cultural zeitgeist. Is that because it might be true — the universe some vast program — or because the idea springs from metaphors thrown off by rapidly advancing computing and AI? From my perspective, it is more likely defensive, in keeping with a long line of unproven, largely metaphysical responses to existential concern. Old wine in new pixels.

item.title: 1 Thing Your Relationship Needs More Than Chemistry
item.description:
Self-Control

1 Thing Your Relationship Needs More Than Chemistry

The trait that makes long-term relationships work is simple and unglamorous.

Posted July 21, 2026

Source: Ba Tik / Pexels

Attraction in a relationship is a measure of intensity. That is, how strongly two people are drawn to each other, how quickly the connection forms and how much energy the relationship generates in its early months. What it does not measure is durability, because durability isn’t tested by attraction. It’s tested by conflict, disappointment, and the accumulated friction of two people living inside each other’s lives for years at a time.

A relationship can score extremely high on chemistry and still fail the only test that determines its longevity, because that test happens later, under different conditions and chemistry was never built to pass it.

The quality that does predict longevity has been hiding in plain sight for over two thousand years, under a name most people associate with philosophy rather than psychology: temperance. Classical thinkers used it to describe the capacity to feel a powerful impulse and choose not to act on it.

Contemporary psychology inherited the same concept and gave it a clinical label, self-regulation, but kept its place among the small set of traits considered foundational to human character.

Where the Trait Actually Operates

Temperance does its work in a specific, recurring moment: immediately after a partner has done something careless, dismissive or unfair, and before the other partner has responded. In that narrow window, an impulse toward retaliation is nearly automatic. It’s easy to snap back with a sharp reply, a withdrawal or even a punishing silence. What happens next depends almost entirely on whether that impulse gets acted on or interrupted.

Relationship researchers refer to the interruption itself as accommodation: the act of inhibiting a destructive response to a partner’s provocation and substituting a constructive one instead. A 2001 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that dispositional self-control was one of the strongest and most consistent predictors identified — people higher in self-control were reliably better at performing this exact substitution, swapping the retaliatory reflex for a response that served the relationship rather than the ego. The finding held across multiple independent studies, which is notable in a field where most single effects don't replicate that cleanly.

A 2020 study published in Aggressive Behavior that tracked heavy-drinking couples over 30 days in their daily lives found a related, if more modest, pattern outside the lab: depleted self-control was linked to more anger and arguing with a partner in the hours that followed, though the authors note the effect was modest and the relationship ran both ways, with arguing also draining self-control in turn.

Why This Trait Outweighs Attraction Over Time

The reason this trait outperforms chemistry as a long-term predictor is arithmetic rather than romantic. A relationship generates thousands of these small provocation-and-response cycles over the course of a decade.

Individually, almost none of them are serious enough to end a relationship. Collectively, they are the relationship, in the sense that they are what most of a long partnership is actually made of. A couple’s trajectory is set less by how often these moments occur and more by which impulse wins each time one does. Chemistry has no influence over that outcome, because by the time the provoking moment arrives, whatever chemistry contributed has already been spent.

The relationship between self-control and good partnership is not perfectly linear, and the research is careful about this. Some of the same investigators who established the link between self-control and accommodation published a 2013 study in Psychological Science finding that people lower in self-control are, in certain circumstances, more willing to make immediate personal sacrifices for a partner — their prosocial impulse fires before self-interest has time to intervene. Self-control, in other words, is not a universal advantage; it is specifically valuable at the moment of provocation, not a trait that should be maximized without limit.

There is a related failure mode worth naming directly: restraint that has curdled into suppression. A partner who never appears frustrated is not necessarily practicing temperance. In some cases, that pattern reflects a partner who has stopped registering their own needs at all, which produces the appearance of equanimity without any of its substance. The clinically meaningful version of this trait is not the absence of a reaction. It is the presence of a brief interval between the reaction and the response, long enough for the better instinct to overtake the faster one.

Can This Trait Be Cultivated?

Unlike attraction, which either exists between two people or doesn’t, this trait has a documented mechanism for strengthening it, and it isn’t willpower. Researchers studying emotion regulation have found that people can widen that crucial interval between provocation and response by changing their vantage point on the moment itself, by stepping back to observe the exchange as an outside witness would, rather than experiencing it entirely from the inside. This is known as self-distancing, and a 2017 review published in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, surveying over a decade of research on it, describes it being tested directly in moments of provocation and romantic conflict, consistently finding less aggressive thinking and fewer aggressive responses in the heat of an argument, and more constructive behavior toward a partner during an actual disagreement, among people who adopt this outside perspective rather than staying immersed in the moment.

The mechanism is not complicated, even if it takes practice to use in real time. It amounts to a shift in vantage point rather than a suppression of feeling. That small relocation of perspective appears to be what creates the interval in the first place.

The trait that predicts whether two people are still together in 20 years operates in a moment attraction doesn’t reach. And unlike attraction, it’s a moment a person has some actual say over.
